member.summary:
Provides helper methods for safely executing async operations synchronously in PowerShell binary cmdlet context.
PowerShell 7+ runs cmdlets without a , so blocking on a task here cannot deadlock the way it would in a UI/ASP.NET classic context. We deliberately do not use Task.Run to keep the call on the cmdlet's own thread — this preserves flow (the ambient slot in particular) and avoids an unnecessary thread-pool hop per await.

member.name: T:PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionDependencyStore
member.summary:
Records which extension contributed which files to a module's bin/{TFM}/ root.
That folder is otherwise a flat pile with no provenance: the module's own dependencies and every extension's dependencies sit side by side, indistinguishable. Without a record an uninstall cannot clean up (deleting a shared assembly would break whatever else needs it), nothing can tell which files are orphans, and a module upgrade — which lands in a brand new version folder — silently loses every extension with no way to report what went missing.
The file lives next to extensions.trust.json and is edited through a JSON node tree so hand-written content survives a round trip. It is bookkeeping, not a trust boundary: a missing or unreadable file only costs provenance, never correctness of loading.

member.summary: Name of the sidecar file, kept beside the trust list in bin/{TFM}/.

member.name: M:PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionDependencyStore.Read(System.String)
member.summary: Reads every recorded extension. A missing file yields an empty set; a malformed one yields an empty set too, because losing provenance must never block an install or an uninstall the administrator asked for.

member.name: M:PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionDependencyStore.Record(System.String,PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionDependencyRecord)
member.summary: Records (or replaces) what one extension contributed.

member.name: M:PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionDependencyStore.Remove(System.String,System.String)
member.summary:
Removes an extension from the record and reports which of its files are now safe to delete.
A file qualifies only when the extension being removed INTRODUCED it — it did not exist in the module beforehand — and no other recorded extension lists it at all. Both halves matter: the first keeps the module's own assemblies untouched, the second keeps a dependency shared with another extension in place.
member.returns: File names that no longer belong to anything.

member.name: T:PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionTrustPolicy
member.summary:
Strong-name trust boundary applied by before an extension assembly is loaded and instantiated. PSDataRepository only loads strong-named plugins whose public key token is trusted. Two sources of trust are combined:
The module's own public key token is implicitly trusted — the in-box providers, formatters and auth extensions are signed with it, and it is the anchor the whole model hangs from.
Additional 3rd-party tokens are added by an administrator to extensions.trust.json (see ).
The policy fails closed: if Core is itself not strong-named there is no trust anchor, so is false and every candidate is denied. An unsigned or untrusted candidate is denied, and the candidate's token is read straight from PE metadata so no code in the candidate runs before the decision is made.
The value is immutable and built once per scan. Trust used to live in a mutable static list that AddTrustedToken could extend at any moment, including midway through a scan, so two candidates in the same load could be judged against different rules. Building it up front also puts the deny reason in one place instead of leaving each call site to phrase its own.

member.name: T:PSDataRepository.Core.Extensions.ExtensionTrustStore
member.summary:
Read/modify/write access to extensions.trust.json, the administrator-managed list of strong-name public key tokens allowed to author plugins.
The file is edited through a JSON node tree rather than being serialised from a POCO so that the explanatory _comment — and anything else an administrator added — survives a round trip. A trust file that silently loses its own documentation the first time a cmdlet touches it would be worse than no cmdlet at all.
This file grants CODE EXECUTION. It records who may author an extension; it says nothing about which contract version an extension targets. Those are orthogonal — a publisher does not become untrusted because their extension needs a rebuild — and the contract version travels with the binary instead, where it cannot drift from the code it describes.
